name: Āśmarathya
summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.20; 1.2.29): the self's identity with Brahman is stated in view of the promise that by knowing one all is known — later read as an early difference-and-non-difference view.
notes: Known only from the Brahma Sūtra and its commentators.

name: Auḍulomi
summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.21; 3.4.45; 4.4.6): the soul is different from Brahman while embodied and becomes one with it on departing — an early form of difference-and-non-difference.

name: Bhartṛprapañca
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin and commentator on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (and reportedly the Kaṭha) Upaniṣad; taught that Brahman is both one and many like the ocean and its waves, that the world is its real modification, and that liberation needs knowledge combined with works. Known only from his critics Śaṅkara, Sureśvara and Ānandagiri.

scholarly.text: before Śaṅkara (6th–7th c. CE or earlier)

notes: The list of eight 'states' (avasthā) of Brahman ascribed to him by Sureśvara is recalled with low confidence and not recorded as a teaching.

name: Bhāskara (Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, the Vedāntin)
summary: Author of the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya that is the classic statement of aupādhika bhedābheda: Brahman really transforms through its power; souls are its parts, distinguished by real adjuncts; liberation after death through knowledge combined with lifelong duty. He attacked Śaṅkara's māyāvāda as Mahāyāna Buddhism in Vedic dress; Vācaspati Miśra and later Advaitins answer him.
notes: Often described as a tridaṇḍin (Vaiṣṇava-style renouncer) — low confidence. Distinct from the mathematician Bhāskara and from Bhāskararāya.

name: Yādavaprakāśa
summary: Advaita-leaning teacher of Kāñcīpuram under whom Rāmānuja first studied; taught svābhāvika bhedābheda (Brahman itself becomes Īśvara, souls and matter). His Brahma Sūtra commentary is lost; the Yatidharmasamuccaya and the lexicon Vaijayantī are attributed to him.

realization_account.text: Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography (Guruparamparāprabhāva) says he disagreed with Rāmānuja's readings, plotted against him on a pilgrimage, and later became his disciple as the renouncer Govinda Jīyar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Śrīvaiṣṇava)

name: Vijñānabhikṣu
summary: 16th-c. Vārāṇasī scholar; in his Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya he interprets the Brahma Sūtras as non-separation (avibhāga) of souls and prakṛti from Brahman — a difference-and-non-difference Vedānta integrating Sāṃkhya-Yoga and rejecting Śaṅkara's māyāvāda (which he calls a crypto-Buddhism, citing the Padma Purāṇa).

name: Nārada
summary: The divine sage; in the Nimbārka line he receives the teaching from the four Kumāras (Sanaka and brothers), who received it from Haṃsa (Viṣṇu as swan), and gives it to Nimbārka (Daśaślokī 6). Gauḍīyas hold Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura to be his incarnation.

name: Nimbārka (Nimbāditya, Niyamānanda)
summary: Founder of the Dvaitādvaita school; author of the Vedāntapārijātasaurabha and the Daśaślokī; taught natural difference-and-non-difference, Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā as Brahman, and the five means culminating in surrender.

realization_account.text: An incarnation of the Sudarśana discus, born to Aruṇa and Jayantī in the Telugu country; named Nimbārka ('sun on the nimba tree') because he held the sun on a neem tree so that a visiting ascetic could eat before sunset; taught by Nārada on Govardhana.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

tradition.text: a former age (tradition gives very early dates)

scholarly.text: variously 7th–13th c. CE; many place him c. 12th–13th c.

name: Śrīnivāsācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Direct disciple of Nimbārka (tradition) and author of the Vedāntakaustubha, the classical commentary on Nimbārka's Brahma Sūtra commentary.

name: Keśava Kāśmīrin Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nimbārka ācārya of Mathurā; author of the Kaustubhaprabhā, the Gītā commentary Tattvaprakāśikā and (attributed) the Kramadīpikā; tradition credits him with defeating rival (tantric) opponents at Mathurā.

name: Śrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Disciple of Keśava Kāśmīrin; author of the Yugalaśataka, Braj verses on the divine couple.

name: Harivyāsadeva
summary: Disciple of Śrī Bhaṭṭa; author of the Mahāvāṇī (Braj songs of the eternal love-play in the sakhī mood) and the Siddhāntaratnāñjali; his disciples spread the school through twelve branches.

name: Paraśurāma Devācārya
summary: Disciple of Harivyāsadeva associated with the Nimbārka seat at Salemabad (Rajasthan).

name: Puruṣottamācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā on the Daśaślokī and the Śrutyantasuradruma on the Kṛṣṇastavarāja.

name: Devācārya
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Brahma Sūtra commentary Siddhāntajāhnavī.

name: Mādhava Mukunda
summary: Later Nimbārka polemicist to whom the Parapakṣagirivajra is attributed.

name: Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Śaiva Brahmasūtrabhāṣya: Śiva with his cit-śakti is Brahman; souls and world are his body; Veda and Śivāgama are equal; liberation is equality with Śiva.

tradition.text: Vīraśaiva authors place him before Śaṅkara

name: Appayya Dīkṣita
summary: 16th-c. polymath of Adaippalam (Tamil country) who revived Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Vedānta in the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā while holding Advaita as final (Śivādvaitanirṇaya).

realization_account.text: Tradition says the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā was written under the patronage of Cinna Bomma of Vellore.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Kriyāsāra, which presents Śrīkaṇṭha's commentary as Vīraśaiva doctrine.

name: Śrīpati Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Śrīkarabhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras, the Vīraśaiva Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita: Śiva and soul, both qualified by Śakti, are non-dual; liberation is liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya.

name: Śivayogi Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, presenting Reṇukācārya's teaching to Agastya on the 101 sthalas.

name: Viṣṇusvāmin
summary: Vaiṣṇava teacher of uncertain date whom the Vallabha tradition counts as the founder of the Rudra Sampradāya in which Vallabha stands; cited by Śrīdhara Svāmin. His own works are lost.
notes: Tradition's account; the historical link to Vallabha is contested. No lineage id exists for a separate Viṣṇusvāmī school, so the tradition's attribution to the Puṣṭimārga is recorded.

name: Bilvamaṅgala (Līlāśuka)
summary: Poet of the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta, revered by Caitanya; placed by the Vallabha tradition in Viṣṇusvāmin's line.

name: Vallabhācārya (Śrī Vallabha, Mahāprabhujī)
summary: Founder of Śuddhādvaita and the Puṣṭimārga; author of the Aṇubhāṣya, Tattvārthadīpanibandha, Subodhinī and the sixteen short works; established the worship of Śrīnāthjī at Govardhana and taught the brahmasambandha initiation.

realization_account.text: Born at Campāraṇya to the Telugu Brahmin Lakṣmaṇa Bhaṭṭa and Illammā; won a debate at the Vijayanagara court and was honoured as ācārya; travelled India three times (the 84 'seats', baiṭhak, mark where he expounded the Bhāgavata); at midnight on Śrāvaṇa śukla ekādaśī at Gokul, Kṛṣṇa appeared and gave him the brahmasambandha, and the next day he initiated Dāmodaradās Harsānī; at the end he took renunciation and entered the Ganges at Kāśī (1531), leaving the Śikṣāślokī as his last instruction.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gopīnātha (elder son of Vallabha)
summary: Vallabha's elder son and first successor, who died young.

name: Viṭṭhalanātha (Gusāṃījī)
summary: Vallabha's younger son and the organiser of the Puṣṭimārga: completed the Aṇubhāṣya, wrote the Vidvanmaṇḍana and Śṛṅgārarasamaṇḍana, elaborated the eightfold daily service (aṣṭayāma sevā), founded the aṣṭachāp of eight poet-singers and emphasised Rādhā (Svāminī); his seven sons founded the seven 'houses'.

name: Dāmodaradās Harsānī
summary: Vallabha's first disciple, initiated with brahmasambandha the morning after the Gokul revelation (tradition).

name: Sūrdās
summary: Blind Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' love and separation (Sūrsāgar); foremost of the aṣṭachāp.

realization_account.text: The Caurāsī Vārtā says Sūrdās, blind from birth, lived at Gaughāṭ near Agra singing songs of humility (dainya) until Vallabha initiated him and told him to sing Kṛṣṇa's play instead; he then sang at Śrīnāthjī's temple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Puṣṭimārga)

notes: Registry id; primary owner U26/U27. Scholarly account: the sectarian link rests on Vallabhan sources only.

name: Kumbhandās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a farmer of Jamunāvato near Govardhana; the tradition remembers his refusal of the imperial court ('what have saints to do with Sīkrī?').

name: Paramānanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' longing (Paramānandsāgar).

name: Kṛṣṇadās Adhikārī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and manager (adhikārī) of Śrīnāthjī's temple.

name: Nanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, author of the Rāspañcādhyāyī and a Bhramargīt.

name: Caturbhujdās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās.

name: Govindsvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and musician.

name: Chītsvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Caube of Mathurā.

name: Gokulnāth
summary: Fourth son of Viṭṭhalanātha, to whom the Caurāsī and Do Sau Bāvan Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā are attributed; head of one of the seven houses.

name: Harirāy (Harirāyajī)
summary: Puṣṭimārga scholar and poet, commentator (Bhāvaprakāś) on the Vārtā literature and author of many Sanskrit and Braj works.

name: Puruṣottama (Puruṣottamajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: The most prolific later Śuddhādvaita scholar: Bhāṣyaprakāśa on the Aṇubhāṣya, Suvarṇasūtra on the Vidvanmaṇḍana, Prasthānaratnākara and many commentaries.

name: Giridhara (Giridharajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Śuddhādvaitamārtaṇḍa is attributed.

name: Bālakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Prameyaratnārṇava is attributed.

name: Mādhavendra Purī
summary: Renouncer revered by the Gauḍīyas as the 'seed' of the love-devotion that Caitanya spread; installer of the Gopāla deity at Govardhana; teacher of Īśvara Purī and (tradition) of Advaita Ācārya and Nityānanda. Tradition places him in Madhva's line.
notes: His lament 'ayi dīna-dayārdra nātha …' is quoted in CC 2.4 (verse number to verify).

name: Īśvara Purī
summary: Disciple of Mādhavendra Purī who initiated Caitanya at Gayā (c. 1508).

name: Keśava Bhāratī
summary: Renouncer who gave Caitanya sannyāsa at Kāṭoyā (c. 1510), naming him Kṛṣṇa Caitanya.

name: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya (Viśvambhara Miśra, Nimāi, Gaurāṅga, Mahāprabhu)
summary: Founder figure of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism: Navadvīpa scholar who after initiation at Gayā led nocturnal congregational chanting, took renunciation, travelled to south India and Vṛndāvana, and lived his last eighteen years at Purī absorbed in Rādhā's love for Kṛṣṇa. His only writing is the Śikṣāṣṭaka; his teaching was given to Rūpa, Sanātana, Rāmānanda and others and recorded by his biographers.

realization_account.text: Kṛṣṇa himself, appearing with the mood and golden complexion of Rādhā to taste her love (CC 1.1.5–6); the hidden (channa) avatāra and yuga-avatāra of Kali who inaugurated the chanting of the name; in his last years he passed through states of divine madness (divyonmāda); he disappeared at Purī in 1533 (accounts differ on how).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nityānanda (Nitāi, Avadhūta)
summary: Wandering avadhūta from Ekacakrā who joined Caitanya at Navadvīpa and led the mission in Bengal; held to be Balarāma; his wives Vasudhā and Jāhnavā and son Vīrabhadra continued his line (Khaḍadaha).

realization_account.text: Balarāma (Kṛṣṇa's brother) appearing as Caitanya's first expansion; famed for delivering the sinners Jagāi and Mādhāi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Advaita Ācārya
summary: Elder Vaiṣṇava scholar of Śāntipur whose prayers, the tradition says, called Caitanya down; one of the Pañca-tattva.

realization_account.text: Mahāviṣṇu and Sadāśiva combined; lived to a great age (tradition: 125 years).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gadādhara Paṇḍita
summary: Caitanya's lifelong companion at Navadvīpa and Purī, identified in the tradition with Rādhā's śakti; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Navadvīpa devotee in whose courtyard the nightly kīrtanas were held; identified with Nārada; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Haridāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Devotee born in a Muslim family (tradition) who chanted three hundred thousand names daily, endured beating in twenty-two marketplaces without abandoning the name, and taught that even the semblance of the name (nāmābhāsa) gives liberation; honoured as the teacher of the name (nāmācārya); died at Purī in Caitanya's presence.

name: Svarūpa Dāmodara
summary: Caitanya's intimate secretary at Purī, whose notebook (kaḍacā) is quoted in the Caitanya Caritāmṛta's opening verses.

name: Rāmānanda Rāya
summary: Governor at Vidyānagara (Godāvarī) and author of the drama Jagannāthavallabha, whose dialogue with Caitanya on the goal and means (CC 2.8) rises from varṇāśrama to Rādhā's love.

name: Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Logician and Advaita teacher at Purī who, after a seven-day Vedānta discussion, became Caitanya's devotee (CC 2.6).

name: Prakāśānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Leader of the Advaita renouncers at Vārāṇasī whom, the Caitanya Caritāmṛta says, Caitanya won over to devotion (CC 1.7; 2.25).
notes: Known for this episode only from Gauḍīya sources; identification with an Advaita author of the same name is disputed.

name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
summary: Formerly Dabir Khās, minister of Sultan Husain Shah of Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Prayāga (CC 2.19); settled in Vṛndāvana; the chief theorist of Gauḍīya devotion: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi, Laghubhāgavatāmṛta, Upadeśāmṛta, dramas and hymns.

name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
summary: Rūpa's elder brother, formerly Sākar Mallik, minister at Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī for two months (CC 2.20–24); author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and the Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī; associated with the Haribhaktivilāsa.

name: Jīva Gosvāmī
summary: Nephew and disciple of Rūpa and Sanātana; the systematic theologian of the school (Ṣaṭ Sandarbha, Sarvasaṃvādinī, Kramasandarbha), grammarian (Harināmāmṛtavyākaraṇa), poet (Gopālacampū) and commentator; leader of the Vṛndāvana community after the elder Gosvāmīs.

name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of a wealthy landholder of Saptagrāma who renounced home, served Caitanya at Purī under Svarūpa Dāmodara and later lived at Rādhākuṇḍa; poet of the Stavāvalī (Manaḥśikṣā, Vilāpakusumāñjali) and exemplar of renunciation and mañjarī-bhāva.

name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of Tapana Miśra of Vārāṇasī; lived in Vṛndāvana as a sweet-voiced reciter of the Bhāgavata; wrote no treatise (tradition).

name: Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of Veṅkaṭa Bhaṭṭa of Śrīraṅgam, where Caitanya spent the rainy season (1511 per tradition); in Vṛndāvana served the Rādhāramaṇa deity (manifested from a śālagrāma); named compiler of the Haribhaktivilāsa and drafter of the Sandarbhas completed by Jīva.

name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta, the Govindalīlāmṛta and the Sāraṅgaraṅgadā commentary on the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta; wrote in Vṛndāvana in old age from the accounts of Raghunātha Dāsa and Svarūpa's notes.

name: Vṛndāvana Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Disciple of Nityānanda and author of the Caitanya Bhāgavata, called the Vyāsa of Caitanya's play.

name: Locana Dāsa
summary: Author of the Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Jayānanda
summary: Author of a Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Murāri Gupta
summary: Physician of Navadvīpa and companion of Caitanya; author of the earliest Sanskrit biography (kaḍacā).

name: Kavikarṇapūra (Paramānanda Sena)
summary: Poet-theologian, son of Śivānanda Sena; author of the Caitanyacandrodaya, the Gauragaṇoddeśadīpikā and the Alaṅkārakaustubha.

name: Śrīnivāsa Ācārya
summary: Second-generation leader who, with Narottama and Śyāmānanda, carried the Gosvāmīs' books from Vṛndāvana to Bengal; the tradition says they were stolen at Viṣṇupur and recovered when King Vīra Hāmvīra became his disciple.

name: Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Second-generation leader from Kheturi whose Bengali songs (Prema-bhakti-candrikā, Prārthanā) shaped Gauḍīya practice; organiser of the Kheturi festival that unified the Bengal community.

name: Lokanātha Gosvāmī
summary: Early associate of Caitanya in Vṛndāvana and Narottama's initiating guru.

name: Śyāmānanda
summary: Second-generation leader who spread Gauḍīya devotion in Odisha.

name: Jāhnavā Devī (Jāhnavā Mātā)
summary: Wife of Nityānanda and a leader of the second generation, who presided at the Kheturi festival and guided the Nityānanda branch.

name: Vīrabhadra (Vīracandra)
summary: Son of Nityānanda and leader of his line at Khaḍadaha.

name: Narahari Cakravartī
summary: 18th-c. author of the Bhaktiratnākara.

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin
summary: Theologian of Vṛndāvana (late 17th–early 18th c.): commentaries on the Bhāgavata, Gītā and Ujjvalanīlamaṇi; Mādhuryakādambinī and Rāgavartmacandrikā on the stages and spontaneous devotion; defender of parakīyā.

name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Orissan scholar trained in Madhva's school who joined the Gauḍīyas; wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya (the school's Brahma Sūtra commentary), Prameyaratnāvalī, Siddhāntaratna and Gītābhūṣaṇa, defending the Gauḍīyas at Jaipur.

name: Śrīdhara Svāmin
summary: Commentator on the Bhāgavata (Bhāvārthadīpikā), the Gītā (Subodhinī) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, blending non-dualism with devotion; Caitanya insisted on respect for him (CC 3.7).

name: Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura (Kedarnath Datta)
summary: Magistrate and writer who revived Gauḍīya learning in the 19th c. (Jaiva Dharma and many works) and identified Māyāpur as Caitanya's birthplace.

name: Gaura Kiśora Dāsa Bābājī
summary: Renunciate bābājī of Navadvīpa, guru of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī.

name: Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī
summary: Son of Bhaktivinoda; founder of the Gauḍīya Maṭha (1920s), who gave renunciation (sannyāsa) a missionary form and criticised premature esoteric practice and caste-based guru lineages.

name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
summary: Disciple of Bhaktisiddhānta; founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (1966), which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra worldwide.

name: Siddha Kṛṣṇadāsa Bābā (of Govardhana)
summary: 18th-c. Braj renunciate associated with manuals (guṭikā/paddhati) of meditative service in the eightfold daily play and the siddha-praṇālī tradition.
